summary: DHCPv6 gives IPv6 hosts addresses and configuration, but its messages can carry identifiers that let others track a device. This informational RFC analyzes the privacy issues of DHCPv6 use by Internet users. It is an analysis of the present situation and proposes no solutions.

eli5.summary: When a computer asks for network settings it may share details that work like a name tag. This paper lists how those tags could be used to follow you around.

subtitle: A catalogue of the DHCPv6 fields and options that can reveal who a device is, what it is and where it has been.

tldr.problem: DHCPv6 messages carry identifiers and options that let observers learn a client's device type, operating system, location, past networks and stable identity.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists the identifiers in DHCPv6 options and fields, reviews existing mechanisms such as temporary addresses, DNS updates and allocation strategies, and maps them to ten kinds of attack.
tldr.outcome: It is an analysis only and proposes no protocol changes; it points to RFC 7844 as one example of such a change.

sections.title: Scope and Terminology
sections.content:
DHCPv6 provides addressing and configuration information to IPv6 hosts. It uses several identifiers that can reveal device type, operating system, and locations the device has previously visited. This RFC discusses those identifiers and the privacy issues they cause, taking pervasive monitoring into account.

Protocol changes are out of scope; the RFC points to RFC 7844 as one such change. The focus is on clients that move between random networks. Servers and relay agents are considered less important because they are typically open for public services.

The RFC defines a stable identifier as any property a client discloses that does not change, or changes very infrequently, and is unique for that client in a given context. Examples are a MAC address, a client-id and a hostname.
sections.eli5: Some of the things your computer says to a network never change, like a name tag you wear everywhere. This paper is about those name tags.

sections.title: Identifiers in DHCPv6 Options and Fields
sections.content:
Many DHCPv6 options carry or hint at identity. The client's source address is a link-local address, which may be based on a physical link-layer address. Each client has a DUID, generated once and kept stable. The default form, DUID-LLT, is based on the link-layer address and is commonly implemented, so the original unobfuscated link-layer address is likely announced even if the address is later randomized. It is carried in the Client Identifier option.

The IAID field of IA_NA, IA_TA and IA_PD options is picked by the client; at least one popular implementation uses the last four octets of the link-layer address. The Client FQDN option can carry a hostname. The Vendor Class and Vendor-specific Information options identify the hardware vendor and can reveal operating system version or memory. The Option Request option, the Client System Architecture Type option, and server-supplied Civic Location and GeoLoc options add further hints.

Relay agents can add the Subscriber-ID, Interface ID, Remote ID, Relay-ID and client link-layer address options. These mostly travel only between relay and server inside the operator's network, so last-hop sniffing usually does not apply, but attacks through the operator's infrastructure do.
sections.eli5: The computer's message is like a form with lots of boxes. Several boxes ask for things like the maker, the model and a number printed on the machine, and each one is a clue.

sections.title: Existing Mechanisms That Affect Privacy
sections.content:
Temporary addresses in DHCPv6 are meant to be used and then left to expire. The RFC calls them nearly useless for that goal because of protocol and implementation issues; for example, clients may mistakenly renew them by reusing the same IAID. Publishing a client's address in public DNS is called a major privacy breach.

DNS updates using the Client FQDN option expose the current address and the hostname. The stable hostname can correlate a client across networks even as its address changes.

Server allocation strategies matter too. Iterative allocation is fast but predictable and makes scanning easier. Identifier-based allocation exposes the identifier in the address. Hash allocation helps only if the hash is implemented correctly, and it does not stop correlation over time. Random allocation is best for privacy, but the client may still leak its MAC address in the Client Identifier option.
sections.eli5: How the network hands out seats matters. If it gives out seats in order, they are easy to guess. If it picks randomly, nobody can predict where you will sit.

sections.title: Attacks Enabled by the Identifiers
sections.content:
Section 5 maps the identifiers to attacks:

  • Device type and OS fingerprinting: vendor options, OUI values, and the combination of options in the Option Request option.
  • Finding location: Civic Location, GeoLoc, Remote ID, Interface ID or Subscriber-ID options, or geolocation of the address prefix.
  • Previously visited networks: a reconnecting client puts earlier addresses in IA Address options.
  • Stable identity: Client FQDN, Subscriber-ID and Client ID can act as long-lived identifiers.
  • Pervasive monitoring: the first DHCPv6 message, SOLICIT, is one of the first packets on a network and can leak identifiers even on an IPv4-only network.
  • IP address or hostname lookup: DNS updates put these in the DNS, and the client ID appears as a SHA-256 digest.
  • Correlation and location tracking: an address built from a stable identifier lets an observer follow a host over time and place.
  • Leasequery and bulk leasequery: an attacker posing as a relay agent or client can pull location data from servers.

The Security Considerations section adds that, in current practice, client privacy and client authentication are mutually exclusive, because authentication reveals more client information.
sections.eli5: Put the clues together and a watcher can guess what kind of computer you have, where you are, and where you have been before.
